title: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases
shortTitle: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases
summary: Internet-wide scanning services probe the routable address space on a schedule and publish the results as a searchable database. A typical record holds the address, the port, the service banner, the certificate offered, and sometimes a screenshot of the login page. An adversary queries those databases by organisation name, address block, or product string, so they can find exposed services without sending a single packet to the victim. Because the data is historical, the attacker compares snapshots over time to see when a host appeared, changed version, or vanished. From the victim side the probing traffic belongs to the scanning provider rather than the adversary, so the visible artefact in firewall logs is the provider crawler. Detection therefore leans on comparing what you expose against what the databases already publish about you.

beginner.definition: Some companies scan the whole internet and publish what they find. Their service records open ports and the software that answers on them. Anyone can search this information by company name. This technique means an attacker reads those results instead of scanning you.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attacker can learn about your internet-facing systems without touching them. That means your firewall sees nothing unusual. If a database already lists an old server with a weak login page, they know where to start. The same data helps you, because you can check what the world can see. Ignoring it means you learn about your own exposure last.
howItWorks: A scanning provider probes every public address on a schedule and records the answers.
The provider stores the port, the service banner, and any certificate it received.
It publishes this data as a searchable website, sometimes with paid access tiers.
The attacker searches by your company name, address range, or a product you use.
They compare older records with newer ones to spot changes and forgotten hosts.
They confirm findings with a small number of direct requests to the listed services.
beginner.example: Imagine a street where a photographer takes a picture of every front door once a month. The photos go into a public album with the house number on each page. A burglar studies the album and picks the door with the oldest lock. The owner never saw the photographer at work. Public scan databases work in exactly that way.
takeaways: Search the public scan databases for your own address ranges on a regular schedule.
Treat anything listed there as information attackers already hold.
Close or authenticate services that you did not intend to expose.

objectives: Explain what internet-wide scan databases contain and how they are built.
Describe why querying them leaves no traffic on the victim network.
Explain how historical snapshots help an attacker track change over time.
Use public scan data to review your own external exposure.
Distinguish provider scanning traffic from adversary scanning traffic.
